newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rate cut puts focus on new central bankers.
newsitem.headline: French rate cut puts focus on new central bankers.

text.p: The Bank of France surprised financial markets by trimming a key interest rate on Thursday, reviving speculation that the appointment of two "doves" may have changed the balance of power on its policy-setting council.
In another surprise, hawkish Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet sought to quell such speculation by issuing a statement that said Thursday's rate cut would be the last for some time.

The central bank lowered its intervention rate to 3.10 percent from 3.15 after a meeting of its monetary policy council, wrongfooting most economists who said earlier this week that the recent rise in the dollar lowered the chances of a cut.

"The Monetary Policy Council considers that our rate for repurchase tenders is presently at the appropriate level in view of the French and international economic environment. The Council has no plans at this stage to change this rate at its upcoming meetings," the Bank of France's statement said.
"This is to kill speculation that the doves are taking over and will take rates below German rates," said David Naude, economist at JP Morgan in Paris.
The Bank has traditionally maintained a small premium over Germany's repo rate to shield the franc from speculative attack.
Smith Barney economist Steven Englander said Trichet, who he believed was reluctant to cut rates on Thursday, was seeking to reassure markets that the Bank was not letting down its guard.
"He's trying to have his cake and eat it," he said of Trichet. "That is, move rates, yet look prudent and not threaten the foreign exchange parities that currently exist."
The franc was unfazed by the cut or the Trichet statement, trading nearly unchanged at 3.3748 per mark at 1950 GMT, but interest rate futures fell sharply in after-hours trading.

Analysts have speculated that the appointment this month of Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard to the nine-member council might have changed the Bank's traditionally cautious policy stance and could lead to faster interest rate cuts.
Both men are seen as close to President Jacques Chirac and reported to favour easier monetary policy. They replaced two men considered staunch supporters of Trichet.
Many economists expected the Bank to take advantage of the expansionary effect of a rising dollar and hold rates steady on Thursday and thus were doubly-surprised by the cut.
But Bank of France watchers said it was too soon to say the cut was evidence of a new monetary stance.

They said they expected the Bank to stick to its pattern of cautious easing and gradually bring the intervention rate down to the three-percent level of Germany's repo rate before currency parities are locked in preparation for European monetary union, due in January 1999.
"This statement doesn't mean that if in three months conditions warrant it, the Bank won't cut rates," Deutsche Bank economist Patrick Mange said.

Some economists dismissed talk about the role of the council's new members as "futile" or "silly" and said the rate cut was simply a continuation of the Bank's tested policy of cautiously lowering rates to boost French confidence and growth.
"It was expected and is in line with the idea of a cautious trend toward the floor level of German rates," said Herve Goulletquer, economist with Banques Populaires.
Industrialists and the centre-right government have been pressing for lower interest rates to boost a sluggish economy and bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment.
The intervention rate was last cut from 3.20 percent, on December 17. The Bank left its five-to-10 day emergency lending rate, considered less important now, unchanged at 4.60 percent.
